column4: Allah sees the Prophet turn his face toward heaven and gives him a qibla that will please him. It directly joins face-direction and rıza before 2:150 completes favor and guidance.
At death the angels strike the faces and backs of those who disbelieve and announce the burning punishment. It is a direct bodily mark of the adverse verdict.
The one Allah leaves astray is gathered on the Day upon his face, blind, mute, and deaf, with Hell as destination. It joins guidance versus straying to an overturned, sightless face.
After 19:58's favored people who fall prostrate, later successors neglect prayer, follow desire, and meet misguidance. It is the immediate contrary line of descent.
Those who are guided receive good speech and are guided to the path of the Praiseworthy (الحميد). It directly reunites the section's حمد with the straight-path image.
A Garden-dweller says that without his Lord's نعمة he would have been among those brought to punishment. Favor is what separates him from the adverse company.
Allah's curse makes them deaf and blinds their eyes. It gives the cursed, wrath-adjacent side a direct impairment of the eye.
A نعمة from Jonah's Lord reaches him so that he is not cast out blameworthy (مذموم). The verse explicitly sets favor against blame, the opposition developed for حمد in the section.
The righteous fear a Day described as frowning and severe (عبوسا قمطريرا). It supplies the grim facial vocabulary immediately before 76:11's radiance and joy.
The dust-darkened faces in 80:40–41 are identified as those of the disbelieving wicked. This ayah supplies the moral identity of that adverse facial scene.
When the Quran is recited to them, they do not prostrate. It is the direct reversal of 19:58 and 17:107–109, where reception of the signs brings faces to the ground.
Some faces have dust upon them. It repeats the section's 80:40 scene of an adverse layer lying upon the face.
Darkness covers those dust-marked faces. It repeats the facial covering that the section reads alongside عَلَيْهِم in 1:7.
The dust-and-darkness faces are identified as the disbelieving, wicked people. It completes the two preceding facial marks with their adverse group.
The Lord will give to the addressee and he will be satisfied (فترضى). The ayah makes divine giving culminate in rıza.
The wording says Allah found the addressee ضالًّا and guided him. Whatever its exegetical scope, its own verbal pairing directly meets the section's guidance-versus-ضلّين concern.
Allah finds the addressee in need and makes him self-sufficient. It gives the gift-side of the section a concrete reversal of lack.
In the calf narrative, Moses calls his people to repentance, and Allah accepts it. This supplies a repentance route out of the calf episode whose wrath is explicit in 7:152.
Obedience to Allah and the Messenger would guide them to a straight path. It is the immediate path-condition before 4:69's company of those favored.
Believers are told not to forbid the good things Allah made lawful and not to transgress. It repeats 20:81's provision joined to a boundary against excess.
The next ayah commands eating the lawful, good provision Allah gives. Its own contribution is the gift whose misuse 5:87 forbids.
After taking the calf, they recognize that they have gone astray and appeal for mercy and forgiveness. It makes misguidance and hoped-for pardon explicit within the wrath narrative.
Moses asks forgiveness for himself and Aaron and asks to be admitted into mercy. The plea follows his angry return and opens the mercy side of the episode.
Yusuf is chosen, taught, and promised the completion of his Lord's favor upon him and Jacob's family. It shows نعمة arriving as election and understanding.
When Yusuf's shirt is placed over Jacob's face, Jacob's sight returns. This reverses the grief-altered eyes of 12:84, though its emotion is reunion rather than anger.
The revealed Book brings people from darkness into light and guides them to the path of the Mighty, Praiseworthy (الحميد). It gives the section's حمد a path-form.
After the gratitude-and-punishment division of 14:7, Moses calls Allah rich and praiseworthy. It distinguishes Allah's حمد from human gratitude or ingratitude.
Whoever is blind in this life is blind in the Hereafter and farther astray from the way. It connects the section's eye imagery to its lost-path side.
Those who repent, believe, and act righteously enter the Garden without injustice. It gives the recovery from 19:59's misguidance its own promised destination.
Allah says the people were tested after Moses and that the Samiri led them astray. It supplies the causal straying behind Moses' angry return in 20:86.
When guidance comes, whoever follows it will neither go astray nor be wretched. It gives the guided alternative to the fall under wrath in the same surah.
The one who turns from the reminder has a constricted life and is gathered blind on the Day. It gives straying a particular adverse eye-state.
Those given knowledge see the revelation as truth that guides to the path of the Mighty, Praiseworthy. It repeats the specific hamd-and-path meeting of 14:1 and 22:24.
Those who feed others say they seek neither recompense nor thanks from them. This gives 76:10–11's feared grim day and granted radiance an ethic that refuses human praise as payment.
The humbled faces are laboring and weary. Its own contribution contrasts exhausted labor with 88:9's face satisfied with its effort.
The laboring, humbled face enters a burning Fire. It supplies the immediate adverse destination for 88:2–3.
The soul addressed in 89:28 is first called tranquil. Its calmness is the inward inverse of the section's anger before the reciprocal rıza is named.
The charitable seeker of the Most High's face will soon be satisfied. It gives rıza as the outcome of an enacted favorable pursuit.
Allah finds the addressee an orphan and gives shelter. It is a concrete prior gift in the sequence whose later result is satisfaction in 93:5.
On that Day people will be questioned about نعيم. It turns the section's favorable gift into an accountable possession within its yawm horizon.
